item.content:encoded:
"I’d love to run again if I had chance": Trump laments 22nd Amendment limits on presidential terms "You know, we have more than two years left. That’s a long time," Trump added. "You can do a lot in that period of time, and you’ve seen the job we’ve done." ANI | Updated: 02-11-2026 23:05 IST | Created: 02-11-2026 23:05 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump admitted he would eagerly seek another term in office if permitted by law, but conceded that constitutional restrictions effectively prevent him from launching another campaign. Speaking to The New York Post’s Miranda Devine on her "Pod Force One" podcast, Trump reflected on his strong polling numbers and expressed a desire to stay on the ballot, while acknowledging the constitutional boundary set by the 22nd Amendment. "I’d love to run again if I had the chance, but the language is very exacting," Trump said, referencing the constitutional rule that limits a president from being elected more than twice. Highlighting his political standing, Trump pointed to internal and public polling to argue that his popularity among voters remains formidable. "They had a poll the other day where I’d beat everybody by so much, I’d love to run, but it’s fine," Trump noted. Rather than fixating on constitutional hurdles, Trump shifted focus to the remainder of his current presidency, emphasising that significant policy achievements are still ahead before his term concludes. "You know, we have more than two years left. That’s a long time," Trump added. "You can do a lot in that period of time, and you’ve seen the job we’ve done." Earlier, Trump intensified his attacks on Democrats over their tax policies, voter identification measures and border security during a campaign rally in Kansas, urging voters to support Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections as the party faces a closely contested battle to retain control of the US Congress. Addressing supporters on Sunday (local time), Trump accused Democrats of opposing tax relief measures, including exemptions on tips, overtime pay and Social Security benefits for senior citizens, while also criticising their positions on voter identification and border security. "Every single 'Dumocrat' in Congress voted against No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, and No Tax on Social Security for our great seniors. They voted against voter ID, proof of citizenship, and securing the border," Trump said. In another sharp attack, the President alleged that Democrats intended to increase taxes, weaken law enforcement and undermine Americans' financial security and way of life. "Democrats want to raise your taxes by trillions of dollars, defund the police, abolish oil and natural gas, wipe out your life savings, bankrupt your family, take away your guns, mutilate your children, and destroy your way of life," he added. Trump also outlined his administration's priorities, including tougher penalties for drug trafficking and human trafficking, measures against corruption and fraud, and stricter voter identification requirements. "We will win the war on corruption and fraud, led by our great Vice President. We will pass the death penalty for large-scale drug dealers, human traffickers, and anyone who kills a police officer. We will pass voter ID, proof of citizenship, and the Save America Act," he said. The Kansas rally came at a crucial moment for Republicans, with the November 3 midterm elections set to determine control of both chambers of Congress and serve as a political test for Trump's presidency. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for election on November 3. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the Senate, where 51 seats are required for a majority, including two independents who caucus with the party. In the House, Democrats need a net gain of three seats to secure a majority of 218. The electoral contest is unfolding against the backdrop of concerns over the cost of living and public dissatisfaction with the President. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
"Building trust requires mutual action": Iran urges Gulf neighbours to stop hosting US military attacks "Iran did not destroy or distort trust," Baghaei stated. "It is not a tactic to do so, and of course they can take a tactic, provided that they decide to abandon the wrong approaches of the past." ANI | Updated: 02-11-2026 22:37 IST | Created: 02-11-2026 22:37 IST

Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Iran

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei responded to criticism from an advisor to the President of the United Arab Emirates regarding eroded trust between Tehran and its Gulf neighbours, placing the responsibility on regional nations that allow their territories to be used for aggressive military actions. Reacting to statements claiming that trust in Iran had been destroyed, Baghaei maintained that Tehran has not engaged in tactics aimed at damaging diplomatic confidence in the region. "Iran did not destroy or distort trust," Baghaei stated during a press briefing. "It is not a tactic to do so, and of course they can take a tactic, provided that they decide to abandon the wrong approaches of the past."Addressing the broader context of recent regional strikes, Baghaei directly connected the ongoing friction over the past eight months to Gulf states permitting US military forces to operate from their soil. He emphasised that Iran retains the right to defend its sovereign territory against actions launched from neighbouring states. "Iran cannot remain silent and not respond to the use of the territory of some countries in the region to attack and encroach on national sovereignty and its people," Baghaei stated. "What happened in these 8 months was the result of the excessive trust and reliance of some countries in the region on the US military presence in their territory," Baghaei said. "Unfortunately, some of these countries not only did not prevent the US from using its capabilities to attack Iran, but also encouraged it."Despite the firm stance on sovereignty and military bases, Baghaei reiterated that Tehran's overarching policy toward neighbouring Gulf states remains rooted in peaceful coexistence and mutual security building, demanding an end to hostility and shared responsibility. "Building trust requires mutual action and mobilisation," Baghaei emphasised. "The Islamic Republic of Iran has repeatedly stated that this is our honest and principled position that we have no enmity with any country in the region. We believe that in order to create sustainable security, the countries in the region must cooperate and build trust with each other." "At the same time, the Iranians' reasonable expectation is that regional countries will not allow their territory and facilities to be misused to attack a large neighbouring country," he added. Furthermore, Baghaei addressed the apparent contradictions in US rhetoric during a weekly press briefing, warning that Tehran will not fall victim to "deception operations" while confirming that Iran remains fully prepared for any eventuality as economic and security conflicts continue. Addressing mixed messages coming from Washington, where hardline rhetoric from President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio contrasts with softer diplomatic correspondence from Vice President JD Vance, Baghaei asserted that Iran approaches the entire process with extreme caution based on past experiences. "Every operation, assuming it is a deception, which is not unlikely from this group, has two sides: one is the deceiver and the other the deceived. Therefore, let us not be deceived and we will not be deceived. This is not our first experience in interacting with the American parties," he added. Baghaei referenced historical military actions, recalling that previous American administrations signalled ongoing diplomatic channels right up until launching strikes, "We have certainly not forgotten that just half an hour before their military aggression on June 13 [1404], the US President tweeted and announced that negotiations with the Iranians were still ongoing. We are aware of what has happened in these two years and also the experience of 2015 and 2018, and we are taking all these matters into account," he said. Analysing the mixed signals emanating from the US ruling structure, Baghaei argued that conflicting statements stem from domestic dissatisfaction with foreign policy decisions tied to Israel. "The fact that there may be different voices at the level of the American ruling body, voices that may sometimes reflect the public demand of the American people to adopt an independent approach to developments in the Middle East, is an issue that we cannot hide. The American society is tired and angry with the Zionist regime's anglophone behaviour towards the United States. We see this both in polls and in the demonstrations that are taking place in the United States," he stated. He further charged that elements within the US government recognise that American interests are being compromised for Israeli strategic ambitions, stating, "Therefore, it is not far-fetched that some people in the American ruling class have come to the conclusion, even if they do not express it or sometimes express it, that America is dedicating its credibility, wealth and position to a party that thinks of nothing else but permanent war in our region." He said that the contradictory stances from Washington create a sense of dilemma for Iran amid the negotiations, asking whether the decisions are being taken from Tel Aviv. "The Zionist regime has proven that its existence is dependent on and conditioned on the continuation of war and bloodshed in the region. With this said, we can consider different points of view; but I emphasise that for us the performance of the American government is important." "These contradictory positions are both a sign of confusion among themselves and also make the international community puzzled as to who is really the main party in the system of governance and decision-making in the United States and who should be talked to in the United States? Do all roads ultimately end in Tel Aviv? This is an issue that America must decide on as soon as possible to maintain its credibility and standing," he added. Responding to concerns over escalating verbal exchanges and the potential for open conflict, Baghaei stressed that Iran already considers itself in an active state of war due to ongoing economic measures and military threats. "The war is underway right now, as we speak. The economic blockade of Iran and the threat against Iran are part of the war that has existed for these eight months," the Foreign Ministry spokesperson asserted. He affirmed Tehran’s readiness to defend its sovereignty regardless of whether diplomatic tracks remain open or stall, "We must be prepared for any eventuality, because the discussion is about defending the homeland, defending the territorial integrity and dignity of a civilised country that is several thousand years old. Therefore, we must be prepared for all scenarios in any situation, whether when our friends are discussing diplomatic processes with mediators or in situations where diplomacy is not ongoing," he added. This comes as The Wall Street Journal reported that an American delegation is expected to join Iranian officials for talks in Doha; he said that Qatar has proposed to reduce the implementation period of Iran’s plan to open the strategic waterway, the Strait of Hormuz, to two days as compared to five. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
Suki Waterhouse confirms she is not yet married to Robert Pattinson, teases "massive" wedding Singer and actress Suki Waterhouse has officially set the record straight on persistent speculation regarding her relationship status, confirming that she and fiancé Robert Pattinson have not secretly tied the knot. ANI | Updated: 02-11-2026 18:36 IST | Created: 02-11-2026 18:36 IST

Robert Pattinson, Suki Waterhouse (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Singer and actress Suki Waterhouse has officially set the record straight on persistent speculation regarding her relationship status, confirming that she and fiancé Robert Pattinson have not secretly tied the knot. After nearly a decade together, Waterhouse addressed the rumours in an interview with the Sunday Times, as cited by E! News, revealing that when they do decide to walk down the aisle, it will be a grand celebration rather than a quiet ceremony. “It would either be all or nothing,” Waterhouse told the publication, adding, “If we were going to go for it we’d have a massive party, blow it out.” The couple, who began dating in 2018 and got engaged in 2023, welcomed their baby girl in March 2024. Waterhouse noted that any potential wedding plans are currently on hold due to their hectic schedules and lack of a permanent home base. Since expanding their family, the duo has split their time across rentals in major cities including London, New York, and Los Angeles. “Our life since having our daughter, which is strange and backwards, hasn’t been anywhere,” Waterhouse shared, adding, “We’ve been in rentals and moving every couple of months, and we just haven’t been home.” Reflecting on their nearly ten-year journey together, the Daisy Jones & The Six star expressed deep gratitude for their bond. “It is almost a decade and that is a beautiful thing,” she said, adding, “It’s a thing that I go, I can’t believe that I have this in my life and I can’t believe that I’m so happy.” (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
"US greatest threat to nuclear non-proliferation regime": Iran blasts Washington over strike threats "The United States is actually the greatest threat to the nuclear non-proliferation regime," Baghaei stated during a press briefing. "The very expression of a threat against a country and the implicit threat that we may use a certain weapon is itself an encouragement to violate the Non-Proliferation Treaty." ANI | Updated: 02-11-2026 17:13 IST | Created: 02-11-2026 17:13 IST

Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Iran

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei slammed the United States on Monday as the single biggest danger to global nuclear non-proliferation on Monday, reacting to American threats targeting Iran’s remaining nuclear facilities. "The United States is actually the greatest threat to the nuclear non-proliferation regime," Baghaei stated during a press briefing. "The very expression of a threat against a country and the implicit threat that we may use a certain weapon is itself an encouragement to violate the Non-Proliferation Treaty." Baghaei expressed regret over the silence of international bodies, including the United Nations, the Security Council, and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in the face of US hostile rhetoric, warning that Washington is setting a dangerous international precedent. He emphasised that "the threats being raised against us will surely make us more determined to strengthen our capabilities in our own defence." Addressing questions on whether Iran might alter its nuclear doctrine in response to military threats, Baghaei noted that public and elite discussions within Iran are a natural reaction to years of American pressure and the targeted assassination of figures linked to Iran's nuclear program. "Iran's nuclear program has been and remains absolutely peaceful, and this has been proven many times," Baghaei affirmed. "The fact that the other side, based on a big lie that began 20 years ago, constantly repeats the claim that Iran has nuclear weapons... fuels this debate as if they have lulled themselves into a dream." However, Baghaei confirmed that Tehran's official stance regarding the treaty remains unchanged for now. "At the decision-making level, we are still a member of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and as long as Iran is a member of this treaty, it considers itself bound and obliged to comply with the obligations contained in that document," he stated. Rejecting calls from IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi for immediate renewed inspections of Iranian nuclear sites, Baghaei accused the global watchdog of taking a biased stance and failing to condemn past attacks on Iranian infrastructure. "We have not reached that stage at all yet," Baghaei said regarding inspections. "Mr. Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency has many debts to Iran and they should settle their previous debts and then talk about the future course." "One of the great debts of the Agency Director General is that they did not take a position in the face of the criminal and illegal action of the United States and the Zionist regime in attacking Iran's nuclear facilities," he added. "Unfortunately, the credibility of the International Atomic Energy Agency has been severely tarnished since then." Baghaei affirmed that any talks regarding future nuclear steps remain strictly contingent on Washington meeting Iran's initial demands through mediated negotiations. His remarks come a day after US President Donald Trump defended the American military action against Iran, saying Washington had acted to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, while describing the rise in oil prices amid the ongoing conflict as a "very small price to pay" for national and global security. Speaking at a rally in Iowa, ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections, Trump reiterated that preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons was the reason behind the US military intervention. "I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon," Trump said. Explaining his decision to undertake military action, he said, "I said, 'let's make that journey into the Middle East because we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon.'" Addressing concerns over rising oil prices due to the conflict with Iran, Trump said the economic impact was justified by the security benefits of the military action. "It's a very small price to pay for the security of this country and for the world," he said. Trump also claimed that Iran had initiated the war and asserted that US military operations had significantly weakened its military capabilities. Trump's remarks come amid renewed discussions between Washington and Tel Aviv over the possibility of resuming military operations against Iran following the US midterm elections. (ANI)
